title: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule open a girls' school in Pune
description: In January 1848 Savitribai Phule, Jyotirao Phule and Sagunabai Kshirsagar started a school for girls at Bhide Wada in Pune, and Savitribai's colleague Fatima Sheikh later opened a school with her in the Sheikh family home.
why_it_matters: Indian feminism starts with a Dalit-Bahujan woman and a Muslim woman claiming education against caste and patriarchy at the same time, so intersectionality here is home-grown, not imported, and education is the first piece of movement infrastructure.

sources.title: Savitribai Phule
sources.note: January 1848, Bhidewada, with Sagunabai; Fatima Sheikh school in 1849

sources.title: Supreme Court allows national memorial to commemorate first girls' school in India
sources.note: 1848, Bhidewada, Budhwar Peth; SC dismissed occupiers' appeal so the Pune Municipal Corporation can build a memorial

sources.title: Activist Dilip Mandal's claim that Fatima Sheikh is a non-existent character is a travesty of historical truth
sources.note: Fatima Sheikh historicity dispute and the evidence for her

confidence: high (year and place); medium (exact day; Fatima Sheikh's role)
caveats: Most sources call this India's first girls' school. Safer wording: 'one of the first girls' schools started by Indians', unless a scholarly history confirms the stronger claim. Fatima Sheikh's existence was publicly questioned in January 2025. Alt News points to a letter Savitribai wrote in 1856 and to books by M.G. Mali (1980, 1988), and it also notes that primary records are thin. Present her with that care. Note for design: the Supreme Court cleared a national memorial at Bhide Wada in 2023.
sensitivity: medium: caste history; the Fatima Sheikh debate is politically charged

title: Tarabai Shinde publishes 'Stri Purush Tulana'
description: Tarabai Shinde's Marathi pamphlet 'Stri Purush Tulana' (A Comparison of Women and Men) turned the tables on writers who blamed women, arguing that men had every fault they pinned on women.
why_it_matters: Calling out double standards has an Indian history of more than 140 years. The pamphlet was met with hostility, written off, and rediscovered only in 1975, which shows why a movement has to archive and amplify women's writing itself.

description: When the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, Article 326 based elections on adult suffrage, so women voted as equals in the first general election of 1951–52, when about 173 million voters were registered.

title: 'Towards Equality' shows how far women had been left behind
description: In 1974 the government-appointed Committee on the Status of Women in India published 'Towards Equality'. It found that independent India had left many women behind, and it drew attention to the declining sex ratio.

Members Vina Mazumdar and Lotika Sarkar also dissented when the committee rejected reserved seats for women in legislatures, a debate that ended with the 2023 Act.

title: The Mathura case sparks India's first national campaign on consent
description: On 15 September 1978 the Supreme Court acquitted two policemen in the custodial rape of a tribal teenager known as Mathura. In 1979 four law professors wrote an open letter, and women's groups campaigned until Parliament changed rape law in 1983.
why_it_matters: It is the template for consent politics: an open letter, new feminist groups such as the Forum Against Rape (1980), street protest and law reform all working together. The 1983 law said courts should presume a survivor did not consent if she says so in custodial-rape cases.

sources.note: judgment date and facts

sources.title: Mathura rape case
sources.note: open letter by Baxi, Kelkar, Sarkar and Dhagamwar; Forum Against Rape (Jan 1980); Criminal Law Amendment Act 1983 (No. 43) and Evidence Act s.114A

caveats: Wikipedia dates the judgment to September 1979, but the judgment record says 15 September 1978, so use 1978. She was a minor, and Indian law restricts identifying rape survivors. 'Mathura' is the name in the public legal record, but use it sparingly and add no personal details.
sensitivity: high: sexual violence against a minor
image_note: No suitable image. Use a typographic 'consent' card. Do not use photos of the survivor.

title: One-third of local council seats reserved for women
description: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, passed in 1992 and in force in 1993, reserved at least one-third of seats in village panchayats and town councils for women. By January 2025 about 14 lakh women were elected panchayat members, 46% of the total.
why_it_matters: It is proof that reservation changes who holds power, and the strongest evidence base for the 2023 law on seats in Parliament.

title: Bhanwari Devi's fight leads to the Vishaka guidelines
description: Bhanwari Devi, a worker in Rajasthan's Women Development Programme, reported being gang-raped in 1992 for trying to stop a child marriage. Women's groups took the issue to the Supreme Court, which on 13 August 1997 laid down India's first binding rules against sexual harassment at work.
why_it_matters: A grassroots worker's courage created rights for every working woman in India. The Court also drew on CEDAW, so global and local feminism reinforced each other.

sources.title: Vishaka and Ors vs State of Rajasthan and Ors, 13 August 1997
sources.note: 'alleged brutal gang rape of social worker'; guidelines to fill the legislative vacuum; quotes CEDAW Art. 11

sources.title: Vishakha and Others v. State of Rajasthan
sources.note: Women Development Programme worker; tried to prevent a child marriage

caveats: The criminal trial of her attackers ended in acquittal (search snippet, not verified). Use the Court's wording ('alleged') or 'reported'. Bhanwari Devi is a public figure who has spoken about the case herself.

title: India's domestic violence law comes into force
description: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 came into force on 26 October 2006. It recognised physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse at home and gave women civil remedies such as protection orders.
why_it_matters: It made the personal legally political. Abuse at home, including control of money, became something a woman could take to court through civil remedies, without starting with a criminal case.

place: New Delhi (Raisina Hill, India Gate, Jantar Mantar)
title: Delhi's December protests rewrite the law on sexual violence
description: After a young woman was gang-raped and murdered on a Delhi bus on 16 December 2012, young people filled Raisina Hill and India Gate. Within weeks the Justice Verma Committee reported (23 January 2013), and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 added offences such as stalking, voyeurism and acid attack.
why_it_matters: Youth-led street protest, plus public suggestions sent to a committee, changed national law in under four months. It is the clearest Indian proof of the protest-to-policy pipeline.

title: The Sabarimala verdict and Kerala's 620 km Women's Wall
description: On 28 September 2018 the Supreme Court ruled that women aged 10 to 50 could not be kept out of the Sabarimala temple. On 1 January 2019 lakhs of women formed a 620 km human chain across Kerala, from Kasaragod to Thiruvananthapuram.
why_it_matters: Equality versus custom inside faith is a live Fourth Wave question, and the chain showed how many women can be mobilised in a single day.

title: Shaheen Bagh: a women-led sit-in in Delhi
description: From December 2019, women in Delhi's Shaheen Bagh, including older women nicknamed the 'dadis', held a round-the-clock road sit-in against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act. It lasted about 101 days, until police cleared it during the Covid-19 lockdown on 24 March 2020.
why_it_matters: It changed who leads protest: homemakers and grandmothers became national political figures (Bilkis made TIME's 100 list in 2020). The Supreme Court later ruled that public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely, which shapes how protest can be organised.

title: Parliament passes the Women's Reservation Act
description: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, received presidential assent on 28 September 2023. It reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, the state assemblies and the Delhi Assembly for women, including within the seats reserved for SCs and STs.
why_it_matters: The 1974 Towards Equality dissent finally became law, but the reservation only starts after a census and a redrawing of constituencies, so 'when does it start?' became the next question.

description: Gisèle Pelicot refused a closed-door trial so that the public could see the case against 51 men, including the husband who admitted drugging her so that she could be abused. On 19 December 2024 a court in Avignon convicted every one of them.

title: Women's reservation is in force but still waiting to start
description: On 16 April 2026 the government brought the 2023 Women's Reservation Act into force. The next day, a constitutional amendment that would have let the quota start after a redrawing of seats based on the 2011 census failed in the Lok Sabha (298 for, 230 against, short of two-thirds). So the one-third quota still waits for a redrawing of seats after the next census.
why_it_matters: This is the unfinished business of Indian feminism. Seventy-six years after equal votes, equal seats are law but not yet working, which gives Gen Z voters a concrete demand they can track.
